title: The Water Footprint of AI
excerpt: Life without batternberg cake is something too horrible to contemplate. Unlike AI, the squares are beautifully and reliably deterministic in their placement and the marzipan surrounding it is truly enhancing to society.
content_html:
Life without batternberg cake is something too horrible to contemplate. Unlike AI, the squares are beautifully and reliably deterministic in their placement and the marzipan surrounding it is truly enhancing to society.


This comparison sounds to me like it is downplaying the significance of the numbers. California's almond-growing is another gross environmental crime, which is regularly controversial in California.


That's because the Californian almond industry is exclusively located in California, unlike the global data centre industry.


Since California produces about 80% of the world's almonds, it also means that the global water footprint for almonds is about the same as the global water footprint for AI.

More directly, a global analysis does not mean the AI data centers are evenly distributed around the world. From the article:

"A Bloomberg analysis suggests about two-thirds of data centers built or planned since 2022 are water-stressed regions, concentrated in Australia, Chile, Mexico, Spain, Saudi-Arabia, and the US Southwest (Nicoletti et al., 2025). Within the United States, Texas hosts over 400 data centers projected to consume nearly 3% of statewide water supply by 2030 (Martinez, 2025), in a state grappling with recurring drought conditions and aquifer depletion."

"Corporate sustainability reports confirm this concentration: approximately 42% of Microsoft's water consumption occurs in water-stress regions, and 15% of Google's water use is concentrated in high water-scarcity areas (Barratt et al., 2025)."

Comparing water-stressed regions in California for almond production to water-stressed regions used for data centers does seem relevant.


I agree with your link that the unsustainable use of water for almond farms causes problems, and agree that these problems are quite similar to that of water use for AI, so both should have high scrutiny. Quoting your link:

> Almonds use roughly the same amount of water as total indoor water use in California. This is unsustainable.

> There are simply too many almonds being planted in areas with unsustainable water supplies (minimal to no groundwater, uncertain or no surface water). ...

> We’re not opposed to growing almonds; we’re opposed to growing them unsustainably and taking water away from the environment and our cities. Almonds are a luxury and export crop; approximately 70% of the state’s crop is shipped abroad for the express benefit of a handful of industrial-scale growers and hedge funds.

> Water is a public trust resource, and Californians must regain control of it as they face a future certain to be beleaguered by drought, low reservoirs and over-drafted aquifers. We can't continue to subsidize agribusiness plutocrats with the water ratepayers need for basic survival.

Water for AI also uses unsustainable water supplies, directs water away from the environment and our cities, and is subsidized for big tech plutocrats paid for by water ratepayers. It also sure seems to me that most AI use falls in the "luxury" category.


It’s always backwards presumption: “No testing for Pfas air or water pollution has yet been done, and companies are not required to report the volume of chemicals they use or discharge.”


Not the original commenter, but assuming its something along the lines of "PFAs are forever chemicals and using them in a data center is going to eventually cause issues when these data centers are taken down and the PFAs stil need to be dealt with"


Did we somehow mass build pure lossy evaporatively cooled data-centres in the AI era while I was asleep ? Most of them im familiar with lose at best 3-4% of their water per day due to recovery systems even when they are evaporative or open loop to a lake. Yet nearly everyone I hear talking about this seems to treat it as if they lose 100% of their water loop contents per day as if it’s a matter-antimatter destruction system…


The paper refers to "indirect water use in electricity generation, and water-intensive semiconductor manufacturing".

Water use in electricity generation is significant. In the England we are in the middle of a drought and it is surprising to realise that electricity generation uses 2.5x more ('environmentally extracted') water than public supply and 10x more than agriculture.


I stumbled on that as well. I thought that water is used to cool but not consumed such as oil is - even I see the ecosystem problem of warm waste water. However, what doesn’t remove drinking water, right?

Even if the water evaporates, it will enter the ecosystem as such and eventually end up as liquid water again. Or am I totally mistaken?


The last datacenter I stepped inside (an FB datacenter in the southwest), they were very proud of how the whole thing operated as a giant swamp cooler. Unclear how they could have been limiting their losses all that much, given the evaporative stacks were open to the outside breeze


The systems used for LLMs are several times more power-hungry than traditional servers. Like, 50-100kW per rack of B200s.


I’m familiar with datacentres, I’ve helped build a few, so I kept up with the new systems, they still aren’t that lossy last time I checked their specs.. however obviously I don’t have access to all the designs popping up in this mad rush.


One can criticize ai data centers but the "water consumption"-argument is by far the least-intelligent one and on track on becoming the same kind of populist urban myth that got Germany cancelling (ie destroying) its nuclear plants in order to... checks notes.... save the world.


The issue with AI datacenters was never about water. Water is an easily dismissable strawman that sloppers love to bring on.

The real issue with AI datacenters is the huge amounts of wasted energy, after decades of energy efficiency efforts.


The eagerness of the corps to switch from "we're all green" to 'fuck Earth with AI' is stunning. I was always suspicious towards the 'corporate left' but this one takes the cake. We must never trust those people again.


What influence do you have over these companies where your trust or distrust matters?

[edit] This is an awfully pessimistic take. Even if these companies will largely do whatever they like, some of us can at least make choices to use alternatives. That is probably what you were getting at.


It’s because the teams in charge of the soft messaging things like ESG are in their own bubble, entirely unconnected to the main business and everyone sorta just ignores them because anyone sane can see it’s not real. It’s like marketing and hr - they’re on their own mission


Companies that attempted for a brief period to pretend to care about climate change. That is a very left wing position among companies!


lol no, if this is the case then we would have banned beef: a grossly inefficient protein source that takes absurd amount of energy and water, and produce significant greenhouse gas waste. We would also ban disposable cheap goods.

Yet we don't.

If people don't like AI, they should just say so, no need to skirt around.


It's not AI, anymore than the Microsoft setup wizard is a sorcerer.

I don't like the snake oil being sold as AI.


I... don’t follow?

LLMs rely on many core AI concepts and techniques: neural networks, backpropagation, transformer inference, etc. An LLM is essentially an implementation of AI.

The term AI has been around since 1955, and has been used by the academics ever since then.

You might not like ChatGPT and co, but they're definitely AIs lol, at least in academic sense.


Additionally, using more water allows datacenters to be more energy efficient because evaporative cooling uses less energy than dry cooling. Datacenters outside of water stressed areas should absolutely being using water because doing so is better for the environment.


I agree energy use is the more concerning issue, while water has probably caught more press because it's more tangible. But there's no getting around thermodynamics. That "wasted energy" is dissipated using large amounts of water.


"Wasted" is a word people use to mean "used for a purpose I personally do not value".

Try persuading people to share your values.


Who could have guessed this would end up with many polarised "massive problem" / "not a problem" comments


Water consumption of AI is a non-issue. Why even spend research and policymaking resources on this?


...I don't think you can declare that something is a non-issue without having spent at least some resources to determine whether it is?


I think one of the more interesting points is this:

> Two-thirds of post-2022 data centers are located in water-stressed regions.

I don't think it's wrong to ask questions about that _IF_ you also ask questions about all the other usages of water, like the Californian almond stuff.

Just saying "You shouldn't use AI because it uses too much water" is kind of ridiculous.


Misconception of the year. If you can guarantee the steam it produces rains down in areas that actually re-join the water cycle easily, you might be right (even though you still have to cover the just in time demand). You can not guarantee that though.

Best regards, European person where lakes dry out atm.


They are not drying up because of AI datacenters and especially not because of European datacenters.

While man-made climate change is undoubtedly real, the yearly "our lakes dry up"-media cycle is not proof of it at all. Check if the return to normal in November will make the news.


>They are not drying up because of AI datacenters

I am aware and never claimed that. Though, the global push towards mega factories, data centers and whatnot does not help the situation. Lots of places here in Germany already struggle with having enough water, so the mindset to "lets just build a Tesla mega factory here" is something I never understood. Can't be that different for data centers. We should use our resources smartly, not for profit margins.


"Our lakes run dry" is a meme at this point. Apparently the doomers entirely forgot their kvetching about Lago di Garda drying out a couple of years ago. Memory-holed doesn't even closely describe this sort of behavior.


Well the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC dried up two times in a row recently, and although there is no direct video evidence, there is a highly credible witness who blames it on almonds and windmills.


I think you mean "re-join the FRESHWATER cycle"? Because obviously it rejoins the global water cycle.


Can someone explain why the data centers are using this insane amount of water. What's the ratio of closed system, evaporation?, and straight-down-the-drain water?


The water use is for cooling and sometimes includes indirect use for electricity generation. But before you call it "insane amounts of water" consider that the 700.000 liters quoted for training GPT-3 is less than 1 time spraying a 9 acres field, which is the size of a tiny hobby farm not a real farm.


The use is definitely for cooling, but I'd also be curious to know what happens to the water later. If it's a closed loop circulation, the water should be returned back to the environment, just warmer than it was originally. Surely that wouldn't be so bad?


I agree that water is an important resource but the wording of "consumption" always rubbed me the wrong way. Is the water contaminated with chemicals? Maybe heat? Can people or wildlife consume it? Can you use rainwater?


> I agree that water is an important resource but the wording of "consumption" always rubbed me the wrong way

While the Earth is (mostly[1]) a closed system when it comes to water, any particular region on Earth is not a closed system with respect to clean drinking water.

Deplete groundwater reserves faster than they refill? No more water for you. Raise the ambient temperature far enough that the rainclouds go somewhere cooler? No more water for you. As long as your usage is below the replacement rate, all seems well. Imbalance the system, and you have indeed "consumed" your local water supply.

> Is the water contaminated with chemicals? Maybe heat?

Typically yes. Definitely yes.

> Can people or wildlife consume it?

With enough water purification infrastructure, sure. I'm not aware of very many datacenters installing such infrastructure.

> Can you use rainwater?

It's all rainwater, whether directly or indirectly. The question is what would have benefited from that rainwater had it not been redirected to a datacenter?

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_escape


> Imbalance the system, and you have indeed "consumed" your local water supply.

Right, but this is not what is reported by "water consumption". It would be much better to have some kind of index (probably multiple) that estimates how close a particular feature of the water system is to a problem. Is the temperature too high, is there too high a concentration of some contaminant, etc etc.


I am not! You said that there are certain tipping points which, when reached, mean that your local water source might be "consumed" - meaning it does not regenerate and goes away permanently. By contrast, in the link you gave (and everywhere else), water consumption means that you used some water. It doesn't say anything about whether you are near a tipping point. They are totally different concepts!


This statistic doesn't show the disproportionate effect it may have on local communities close to these AI datacenters.

blocks.html_en:
> I agree that water is an important resource but the wording of "consumption" always rubbed me the wrong way

While the Earth is (mostly[1]) a closed system when it comes to water, any particular region on Earth is not a closed system with respect to clean drinking water.

Deplete groundwater reserves faster than they refill? No more water for you. Raise the ambient temperature far enough that the rainclouds go somewhere cooler? No more water for you. As long as your usage is below the replacement rate, all seems well. Imbalance the system, and you have indeed "consumed" your local water supply.

> Is the water contaminated with chemicals? Maybe heat?

Typically yes. Definitely yes.

> Can people or wildlife consume it?

With enough water purification infrastructure, sure. I'm not aware of very many datacenters installing such infrastructure.

> Can you use rainwater?

It's all rainwater, whether directly or indirectly. The question is what would have benefited from that rainwater had it not been redirected to a datacenter?

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_escape

blocks.html_en:
> I agree that water is an important resource but the wording of "consumption" always rubbed me the wrong way

While the Earth is (mostly[1]) a closed system when it comes to water, any particular region on Earth is not a closed system with respect to clean drinking water.

Deplete groundwater reserves faster than they refill? No more water for you. Raise the ambient temperature far enough that the rainclouds go somewhere cooler? No more water for you. As long as your usage is below the replacement rate, all seems well. Imbalance the system, and you have indeed "consumed" your local water supply.

> Is the water contaminated with chemicals? Maybe heat?

Typically yes. Definitely yes.

> Can people or wildlife consume it?

With enough water purification infrastructure, sure. I'm not aware of very many datacenters installing such infrastructure.

> Can you use rainwater?

It's all rainwater, whether directly or indirectly. The question is what would have benefited from that rainwater had it not been redirected to a datacenter?

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_escape

content_html_zh: 没有巴特恩伯格蛋糕的生活真是太可怕了，难以想象。 与人工智能不同的是，这些方块的位置具有美丽且可靠的确定性，而围绕它的杏仁糖确实对社会有促进作用。在我看来，这种比较似乎低估了数字的重要性。 加州的杏仁种植是另一项严重的环境犯罪，在加州经常引起争议。这是因为加州杏仁产业仅位于加州，与全球数据中心产业不同。由于加州生产了全球约80%的杏仁，这也意味着杏仁的全球水足迹与人工智能的全球水足迹大致相同。更直接地说，全球分析并不意味着人工智能数据中心均匀分布在全球各地。 文章摘自：“彭博社的一项分析表明，自 2022 年以来建成或规划的数据中心中约有三分之二是缺水地区，集中在澳大利亚、智利、墨西哥、西班牙、沙特阿拉伯和美国西南部（Nicoletti 等人，2025）。 在美国，德克萨斯州拥有 400 多个数据中心，预计到 2030 年将消耗全州供水量的近 3%（Martinez，2025），该州正在努力应对反复出现的干旱条件和含水层枯竭的问题。”“企业可持续发展报告证实了这一集中情况：微软大约 42% 的用水量发生在缺水地区，而 Google 15% 的用水量集中在高度缺水的地区（Barratt 等人，2025）。“将加利福尼亚州杏仁生产用水紧张的地区与数据中心用水紧张的地区进行比较似乎确实相关。我同意你的链接，即杏仁农场不可持续的用水会导致问题，并同意这些问题与人工智能的用水问题非常相似，因此两者都应该受到严格审查。 引用您的链接：> 杏仁消耗的水量与加利福尼亚州室内总用水量大致相同。 这是不可持续的。> 在供水不可持续的地区种植了太多的杏仁（地下水很少甚至没有，地表水不确定或没有）。 ...> 我们不反对种植杏仁；我们不反对种植杏仁。我们反对以不可持续的方式种植它们，并反对从环境和城市中夺走水。 杏仁是一种奢侈的出口作物；该州大约 70% 的农作物被运往国外，为少数工业规模种植者和对冲基金带来明显利益。> 水是一种公共信托资源，加州人必须重新控制它，因为他们面临的未来肯定会受到干旱、水库不足和含水层透支的困扰。 我们不能继续用纳税人基本生存所需的水来补贴农业企业富豪。人工智能用水还使用不可持续的供水，将水引离环境和我们的城市，并由纳税人支付给大型科技富豪的补贴。 在我看来，大多数人工智能的使用都属于“奢侈”类别。这始终是一种倒退的假设：“尚未对 Pfa 空气或水污染进行测试，公司也无需报告其使用或排放的化学品数量。”不是最初的评论者，但假设其内容类似于“PFA 永远是化学品，在数据中心使用它们最终会在这些数据中心被拆除时导致问题，并且 PFA 仍然需要处理”在人工智能时代，当我睡着的时候，我们是否以某种方式大规模建造了纯有损蒸发冷却数据中心？ 据我所知，大多数水体每天最多会因回收系统而损失 3-4% 的水，即使它们是蒸发的或开环进入湖泊的。 然而，几乎所有我听到谈论这个问题的人似乎都把它当作每天失去 100% 的水循环内容物，就好像这是一个物质-反物质破坏系统……该论文提到“发电中的间接用水和耗水型半导体制造”。发电中的用水量很大。 在英格兰，我们正处于干旱之中，令人惊讶的是，发电用水量是公共供水量的 2.5 倍（“环境提取”），是农业用水量的 10 倍。我也偶然发现了这一点。 我认为水是用来冷却的，但不像石油那样被消耗——即使我看到了温暖废水的生态系统问题。 然而，什么并不能消除饮用水，对吧？即使水蒸发了，它也会进入生态系统，最终再次成为液态水。 或者我完全错了？我走进的最后一个数据中心（位于西南部的 FB 数据中心），他们对整个数据中心作为一个巨大的沼泽冷却器的运行方式感到非常自豪。 考虑到蒸发烟囱向外界微风开放，不清楚他们如何能够如此有限地限制损失法学硕士所使用的系统比传统服务器耗电数倍。 例如，每个 B200 机架 50-100kW。我熟悉数据中心，我帮助建立了一些数据中心，所以我跟上了新系统，当我上次检查他们的规格时，它们仍然没有那么有损。 但显然我无法接触到在这股疯狂的热潮中出现的所有设计。人们可以批评人工智能数据中心，但“水消耗”这一论点是迄今为止最不明智的论点，并且正在成为一种民粹主义城市神话，这种神话让德国取消（即摧毁）其核电站，以...... 检查笔记.... 拯救世界。人工智能数据中心的问题从来都不是水的问题。
